e-3858.knowledge_point: The Period of a Transformed Function
e-3858.problem: What is the period of the function $y = 4\sec\left(2x-1\right)-5?$
e-3858.worked_solution:
Given a function of the form $y = A\sec(Bx +C) + D,$ the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{B}.$

In our case, we have that $B=2.$ Therefore, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi.$

e-3860.knowledge_point: Finding the Range of a Transformed Function
e-3860.problem: Find the range of the function $y = -2\csc(3x+5)-1.$
e-3860.worked_solution:
The range of $\csc x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\csc x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup  [1, \infty)
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\csc\left(3x+5 \right) \in (-\infty, -1] \cup  [1, \infty).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\csc\left(3x+5 \right)\leq -1, \qquad \csc\left(3x+5 \right)\geq 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $-2$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)\le -1 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)\ge 2 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)-1\ge 2-1 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)-1\ge 1 \\  & f(x)\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $-2$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)\ge 1 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)\le -2 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)-1\le -2-1 \\  & -2\operatorname{csc}⁡(3x+5)-1\le -3 \\  & f(x)\le -3.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x) \geq 1, \qquad f(x) \leq -3.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty, -3] \cup [1, \infty).$

after.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+1.$
after.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- If we add $1$ to the first interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\le -1 \\  & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+1\le -1+1 \\  & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+1\le 0 \\  & f(x)\le 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If we add $1$ to the second interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\ge 1 \\  & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+1\ge 1+1 \\  & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+1\ge 2 \\  & f(x)\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le 0,\,f(x)\ge 2.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,0]\cup [2,\infty ).$

after.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4.$
after.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\le -1,\,\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- If we add $4$ to the first interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\le -1 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\le -1+4 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\le 3 \\  & f(x)\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

- If we add $4$ to the second interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\ge 1 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\ge 1+4 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\ge 5 \\  & f(x)\ge 5.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le 3,\,f(x)\ge 5.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,3]\cup [5,\infty ).$

content.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4.$
content.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\le -1,\,\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- If we add $4$ to the first interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\le -1 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\le -1+4 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\le 3 \\  & f(x)\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

- If we add $4$ to the second interval, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)\ge 1 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\ge 1+4 \\  & \operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-1)+4\ge 5 \\  & f(x)\ge 5.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le 3,\,f(x)\ge 5.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,3]\cup [5,\infty ).$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2.$
after.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $-1$ and adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\ge 1+2 \\  & f(x)\ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $-1$ and adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\le -1+2 \\  & f(x)\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\ge 3,\,f(x)\le 1.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,1]\cup [3,\infty ).$

content.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2.$
content.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $-1$ and adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\ge 1+2 \\  & f(x)\ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $-1$ and adding $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\ge 1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})\le -1 \\  & -\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x-\frac{\pi }{4})+2\le -1+2 \\  & f(x)\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\ge 3,\,f(x)\le 1.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,1]\cup [3,\infty ).$
